teaser: Nearly blind, widowed, with a war on: Monet answered by ordering canvases over four meters wide.
review_notes:
Museum dating is c. 1915-26; the catalog year 1920 is a midpoint.
This is the left panel of the Agapanthus triptych; center panel at the Saint Louis Art Museum, right panel at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City.
Agapanthus plants originally painted at lower left and later painted out by Monet (technical studies): check.
Panel size approx. 2 x 4.25 m; triptych about 12.8 m wide.
Alice died 1911, cataract diagnosis 1912, Jean died 1914, large studio built 1915-16, surgery on the right eye in 1923.
Offer to the French state the day after the Armistice (letter to Clemenceau, 12 November 1918).
Cleveland acquired its panel in 1960.
Monet ordering his paint tubes by position because of his failing color vision: commonly reported, check.
The source image is small and includes the frame, so the interactive blocks point only at large regions.

lesson.text: Take stock of Claude Monet around 1915. His wife Alice had died in 1911. His elder son Jean followed in 1914. Doctors had found cataracts, a clouding of the lens, in both his eyes. And a world war was being fought a few hours from his garden gate.

He was in his mid-seventies and rich. He could have stopped. What he did was build a new studio the size of a barn, with a glass roof, and order canvases two meters high and more than four meters wide (about 6.5 by 14 feet). This is one of them.
The canvases were too large to carry to the pond. Monet had them mounted on rolling easels so that he could push them around the studio and line them up side by side.

That detail matters, because this painting is only a third of a thought. It is the left panel of a triptych, a work made of three parts. Side by side, the three stretched nearly thirteen meters (42 feet), wide enough to fill your whole field of vision.
At that scale Monet stopped describing a pond and started building an environment. He worked from memory and from smaller studies, far from the water, with the pond rebuilt in paint around him.

spots.title: Lilies in light
spots.text: A drift of pads near the top, touched with pink, pale blue and cream. The surrounding water is violet, so this group seems to catch the last sun.

spots.title: Pale rings
spots.text: On the left, pads are reduced to loose pale ovals with nothing inside. Monet draws them with the brush in a single turn of the wrist.

spots.title: Green depths
spots.text: The lower half turns green and streaky. It can be read as long grasses on the bank or as weeds seen through the water. Monet does not decide for you.

spots.title: White blooms
spots.text: At the lower right, a few firm white flowers sit on dark water. Their curved strokes are the most solid things in the whole panel.

lesson.text: You probably noticed there is nowhere to stand. No bank, no edge, no sky: violet above, green below, and things floating in between. Painters forty years later would call this an all-over picture, one with no center and no frame inside the frame.
The title is a ghost. Agapanthus, a tall plant with blue flower heads, once stood in the lower left corner of this panel. Monet later painted it out, but the name stuck to the whole triptych.

His eyes were failing through all of this. Cataracts filter out blues and violets and turn the world yellowish and dim. Monet arranged his tubes in a fixed order so he could choose colors by position, and he put off surgery until 1923. So where, in this cool painting, does he allow himself any warmth?
Almost everything here is violet, blue or green. Find the one small flare of yellow and orange.

spots.title: A single warm note
spots.text: Two or three dabs of yellow and orange among the white lilies at the lower right. In four meters of cool color they work like a struck match.

lesson.text: The late Water Lilies are not views of a pond. They are rooms of paint, made to surround you so completely that the edges stop mattering.

The day after the fighting stopped in November 1918, Monet offered large pond paintings to France as a monument to peace. That gift became the oval rooms of the Orangerie in Paris. This triptych was left out and stayed in his studio when he died in 1926.

Nobody wanted it for decades. In the 1950s, as huge abstract canvases made late Monet look modern again, the triptych was sold in pieces. Its three panels now live in three cities: Cleveland, St. Louis and Kansas City.

quiz.question: What is a triptych?
options: A work made of three parts
quiz.explanation: This canvas is the left panel of three.

quiz.question: Why is the work called Agapanthus?
options: It was painted in a town of that name
The plant once appeared at the lower left before Monet painted it out
It was the name of his gardener
quiz.explanation: The plant is gone but the title remained.

quiz.question: What eye condition affected Monet while he painted these panels?
quiz.explanation: Cataracts clouded his lenses and dulled blues and violets.

quiz.question: How could Monet move such enormous canvases around?
options: They were mounted on rolling easels
They were painted on the floor
Assistants carried them to the pond each day
quiz.explanation: Rolling easels let him line the panels up in the studio.

quiz.question: Where are the three panels today?
options: All in the Orangerie in Paris
quiz.explanation: Cleveland, St. Louis and Kansas City each own one.

facts.text: Monet painted this panel outdoors at the edge of the pond.
facts.explanation: It was too large to move outside and was painted in his big studio.

facts.text: Monet offered large water lily paintings to France the day after the 1918 armistice.
facts.explanation: That gift became the rooms of the Orangerie.

facts.text: This triptych was installed in the Orangerie with the others.
facts.explanation: It stayed in his studio and was sold decades later.
